issues.legal_issue: A civil proceeding and an independent criminal investigation concerning related facts may proceed simultaneously, and the civil proceeding alone does not justify staying the investigation.
material_facts: A civil suit for specific performance was dismissed after the trial court found that a receipt relied on to establish an additional payment and delivery of possession was forged or not proved authentic.
The property owner lodged a criminal complaint alleging that the receipt was fabricated, and the police registered a case and began an investigation.
During the appeal from the civil judgment, the High Court stayed the criminal investigation.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not correct in staying the investigation; the civil appeal and the criminal investigation could proceed simultaneously.
issues.legal_principle: Whether civil or criminal proceedings should be stayed depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. There is no general bar to simultaneous proceedings, and findings in one proceeding are not final or binding in the other because the standards of proof differ. The Court relied on M.S. Sheriff v. State of Madras, Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, and Institute of Chartered Accountants of India v. Assn. of Chartered Certified Accountants. It distinguished Mahar Jahan v. State of Delhi, which concerned a summary possession proceeding under Section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure while a civil suit concerning possession was pending.

predicates.civil_criminal_parallel_case: A civil proceeding and a criminal proceeding concerning related events are both pending.
predicates.criminal_investigation_independently_all: The criminal investigation concerns an allegation that a document involved in the civil dispute was forged.

issues.definition: When related civil and criminal proceedings are pending and the criminal investigation independently concerns alleged document forgery, the investigation may continue alongside the civil proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: The court-complaint restriction for offences involving forged documents applies when the forgery occurs after the document has been produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding.
material_facts: The criminal complaint alleged that the receipt was fabricated before it was relied on in the civil suit.
The receipt was subsequently filed in the civil proceeding, and the trial court considered whether it was forged.
The High Court stayed the investigation into the alleged fabrication.
issues.conclusion: The restriction did not prevent the criminal investigation because the alleged forgery was of a document later produced in court, rather than an offence committed after the document entered court custody.
issues.legal_principle: Section 195(1)(b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal Procedure applies only when an enumerated offence concerning a document is committed after the document has been produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding, while it is in custodia legis. The Court relied on the Constitution Bench decision in Iqbal Singh Marwah v. Meenakshi Marwah, which approved Sachida Nand Singh and rejected an interpretation that would shield a person who forged a document before arranging for it to be filed in court.

predicates.criminal_case_concerns_document_forgery: The criminal proceeding concerns an allegation that a document was forged.
predicates.document_was_allegedly_forged_before_cou: The alleged forgery occurred before the document was produced or given in evidence in a court proceeding.

issues.definition: If a criminal proceeding concerns alleged document forgery that occurred before the document was produced in court, the court-complaint restriction does not bar that proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: An interim arrangement allowing a party to remain in possession of disputed property subject to periodic payments need not be disturbed when the party asserts substantial payments and has made substantial deposits.
material_facts: While an appeal from dismissal of a specific-performance suit was pending, the High Court allowed the respondent to remain in possession of the theatre subject to monthly deposits.
The respondent asserted that it had paid substantial sums toward the transaction, apart from the disputed payment, and had made substantial deposits.
The appellant challenged the interim arrangement in the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The interim order, as modified, was not disturbed, and the appeal challenging it was dismissed; the Court stated that it had not decided the merits of the civil appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court concluded, in view of the circumstances—particularly the respondent's asserted payments and deposits—that the interim order need not be interfered with. It did not determine the merits of the underlying dispute or state a broader statutory rule.

predicates.appeal_challenges_interim_property_arran: An appeal challenges an interim arrangement concerning disputed property while a civil appeal is pending.
predicates.party_allowed_to_remain_in_possession: The interim arrangement allows one party to remain in possession of the disputed property subject to conditions.
predicates.party_asserts_substantial_payments_and_h: The party permitted to remain in possession asserts substantial payments connected to the dispute and has made substantial deposits under the interim arrangement.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an interim property arrangement that permits a party to remain in possession, and that party asserts substantial payments and has made substantial deposits, the arrangement is left undisturbed.
